[THALABI:v4p18/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · ابن عمر | reports | Ibn ʿUmar reports that the Prophet loudly ordered dogs killed; people killed dogs encountered with a woman coming from Madina, and the Prophet prohibited their sale price.

[THALABI:v4p18/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | After people asked what dog-caught prey remained lawful, the verse permitted useful dogs, forbade keeping useless ones, ordered harmful or rabid dogs killed, and spared harmless dogs.

[THALABI:v4p18/r7] THALABI, d. 427 · عمرو بن عبيد | reports | Asked why a nonworking dog reduces reward, ʿAmr b. ʿUbayd explains that it barks at guests and frightens petitioners.
[THALABI:v4p19/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | Generous Arabs disliked and condemned tethering dogs because dogs barked at guests and frightened petitioners, and they wanted to kill them.

[THALABI:v4p19/r11] THALABI, d. 427 · ابن مسعود وأبو زرين والحسن | reports | Ibn Masʿūd, Abū Zurayn, and al-Ḥasan read مكلبين with a light lām, in the sense of training or urging the hunting animal.
[THALABI:v4p19/r12] THALABI, d. 427 · الحسن والقتيبي | reports | Al-Ḥasan and al-Qutaybī also derive the word from أكلب, meaning someone acquired many dogs; dogs are named because they are most common, while all trained predators are intended.
[THALABI:v4p19/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · بعض شعراء البصرة | reports | An unnamed Basran poet jokes that the dogs at ʿAmmār's lodging nearly devoured the visitors, illustrating the social nuisance of barking dogs.
[THALABI:v4p19/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · سعيد بن جبير | reports | Saʿīd b. Jubayr says the verse was revealed about ʿAdī b. Ḥātim and Zayd al-Khayl, later named Zayd al-Khayr, who asked about hunting dogs and falcons.
[THALABI:v4p19/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · عدي بن حاتم وزيد الخير | reports | The two hunters asked about prey caught by their dogs and falcons: some animals could be slaughtered in time, while others died before they could be slaughtered, though carrion was forbidden.
[THALABI:v4p19/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | In the verse, الطيبات means lawful slaughtered animals, and ما علمتم means prey caught by trained hunting animals.
[THALABI:v4p19/r6] THALABI, d. 427 · author | rejects | One view permits only prey reached in time for slaughter and forbids prey killed beyond reach; the author says this position is not acted upon.

[THALABI:v4p19/r9] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The accusative مكلبين describes the state of hunting with trained dogs; taklīb means inciting or setting the animal onto prey.

[THALABI:v4p20#2/r8] THALABI, d. 427 · سعد بن أبي وقاص | reports | Saʿd says his fierce hunting dogs eat from their catch and that one may eat what remains, even if only half or two-thirds is left.

[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:5:4/r4] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | The trained hunting creatures are catchers among birds, dogs, and predatory beasts.
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:5:4/r5] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | Mukallibin describes training the hunting animals to hunt.
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:5:4/r6] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | Teaching the animals means disciplining them to pursue prey.
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:5:4/r7] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | One may eat prey the trained animal kills if it does not eat from it; if it eats from the prey, it is apparently forbidden.
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:5:4/r8] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | God's name is mentioned when the hunting animals are released.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p293/r1] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | Poets may independently share broad subjects such as praising courage, generosity, beauty, or a horse’s speed; this agreement is not borrowing.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p293/r2] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | A poet may establish a quality through a familiar comparison, such as likening courage to a lion or generosity to a sea.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p293/r3] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | Poets also infer qualities from characteristic behavior: a composed, smiling warrior or a generous person welcoming petitioners cheerfully.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p293/r4] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | rejects | Al-Jurjani rejects treating shared praise topics as theft; such accusations mistake common premises, like bravery being praiseworthy, for one poet’s invention.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p293/r5] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | Shared ways of proving a trait, such as lion-courage or sea-generosity comparisons, are common knowledge embedded in reason and custom, regardless of era.
[DAMGHANI:v1p235/r2] DAMGHANI, d. 478 · author | holds | Sarīʿ al-ḥisāb can mean that the reckoning has arrived; the source gives a parallel in al-Baqara. | mentions 2:202
[DAMGHANI:v1p302/r1] DAMGHANI, d. 478 · author | holds | Al-ṭayyibāt can mean lawful things, including the crops and livestock the pre-Islamic Arabs used. | mentions 7:32
[DAMGHANI:v1p302/r6] DAMGHANI, d. 478 · author | holds | Al-ṭayyibāt can mean animals slaughtered as food and made lawful for people. | mentions 5:5
[JISHUMI:v3p1873/r1] JISHUMI, d. 494 · ابن مسعود والحسن | reports | The common reading has mُkallibīn with a doubled lām; Ibn Masʿūd and al-Ḥasan read it without doubling, which may mean the same thing or refer to someone with many dogs.
[JISHUMI:v3p1873/r10] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Al-ṭayyibāt is nominative as the passive verb's subject; with the active reading aḥalla, it would be accusative as the object.
[JISHUMI:v3p1873/r11] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | reports | Min in mimma amsakna is partitive because only some of the prey is lawful, not its entrails and blood.
[JISHUMI:v3p1873/r12] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | reports | Another grammatical view takes min as an emphatic extra particle, with a parallel phrase at 39:7. | mentions 39:7
[JISHUMI:v3p1873/r2] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Ṭayyib means the opposite of foul, lawful and wholesome, or pleasant; ḥalāl, ṭayyib, ṭalq, and mubāḥ are near-synonyms, though mubāḥ implies an authorizer.
[JISHUMI:v3p1873/r3] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Jawāriḥ are hunting earners among predatory birds and other animals; the singular is jāriḥ.
[JISHUMI:v3p1873/r4] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | The word for limbs is related to earning because limbs are used to acquire misdeeds; ijti rāḥ means work or acquisition, linked to 45:21. | mentions 45:21

[JISHUMI:v3p1873/r6] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | A rabid dog has a madness-like disease; a bitten human can also be called kalb, and kalab describes hardship by comparison with the dog's severity.
[JISHUMI:v3p1873/r7] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | reports | One parsing makes mā the subject and dhā its predicate, meaning “what is the thing that was made lawful for them?”
[JISHUMI:v3p1873/r8] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | reports | Another parsing treats mādhā as one nominative noun, with uḥilla as its predicate: “what was made lawful for you?”
[JISHUMI:v3p1873/r9] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Mukallibīn is an accusative circumstantial phrase: the addressees are in the state of becoming owners of trained dogs.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v2p5#3/r2] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · أبو ميسرة | reports | Abū Maysara says this sura contains eighteen rulings not revealed together elsewhere, including forbidden carrion, trained hunting animals, food and marriage with People of the Book, purification, theft, hunting in consecration, and testimony at death. | mentions 5:3, 5:4, 5:5, 5:6, 5:38, 5:94, 5:103, 5:106
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v3p15#2/r1] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | reports | One view defines the lawful good things as slaughtered animals over which God's name was pronounced; another includes anything Arabs find pleasant unless Qurʾān or Sunna forbids it.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v3p15#2/r10] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | A beast counts as trained when it responds to release and restraint and holds rather than eats prey; after this is observed repeatedly, at least three times, its catch is lawful when sent by its owner.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v3p15#2/r11] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim reports: eat prey killed by a named, trained dog; refuse prey it eats or that is caught with uninvoked dogs, and avoid game found in water, while a wound from one's arrow alone remains lawful even if found later.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v3p15#2/r2] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · الضحاك والسدي | reports | They restrict hunting beasts to dogs and require ritual slaughter for prey caught by other animals; the author says this view is not followed.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v3p15#2/r3] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · جمهور أهل العلم | reports | The majority take jawāriḥ as trainable hunting predators, including beasts such as cheetahs, leopards, and dogs and birds such as hawks, eagles, and falcons; prey from all is lawful.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v3p15#2/r4] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | Jawāriḥ are so called because they earn their owners' sustenance from hunting; the root can mean to earn, as in calling a family's breadwinner its jāriḥa.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v3p15#2/r5] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | Mukallib is one who incites dogs to hunt or trains them; kilāb can mean dog-owner or a hunter using dogs.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v3p15#2/r6] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | Mukallibīn is accusative as a circumstantial phrase, describing the handlers as they set the beasts onto prey; dogs are named because they are most common, though all hunting animals are meant.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v3p15#2/r7] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | Training means teaching the beasts the etiquette of taking prey.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v3p15#2/r8] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · السدي | reports | Al-Suddī interprets the phrase as meaning as God taught you, with min functioning like the particle kāf.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v3p15#2/r9] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | A trained animal's catch is lawful if it goes out when released by its owner and catches and kills the prey.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v3p15/r1] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · سعيد بن جبير | reports | Saʿīd ibn Jubayr says the verse was revealed about ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim and Zayd al-Muhalhil al-Ṭāʾī, known as Zayd al-Khayl and renamed Zayd al-Khayr, who asked about hunting with dogs and falcons.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v3p15/r2] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | reports | Another account says the verse answered people who asked what could be used from the dogs the Prophet had ordered killed; he then allowed keeping useful dogs and forbade keeping useless ones.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v3p15/r3] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Abū Hurayra reports that keeping a dog except for livestock, hunting, or crops diminishes one's reward by a qīrāṭ each day.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v3p15/r4] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | prefers | The first account is the sounder explanation for the verse's occasion of revelation.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v3p17/r1] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | Pronouncing God's name is required over slaughter at the time of slaughter and in hunting when releasing the animal or shooting the arrow.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v3p17/r2] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Anas reports that the Prophet sacrificed two speckled, horned rams with his own hand, saying God's name and the takbīr while placing his foot on their sides.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p640#2/r1] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | ‘Trainers’ is a circumstantial accusative modifying ‘you have trained’; it indicates a highly skilled expert in training hunting animals.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p640#2/r2] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | ‘Teaching them’ is either a second circumstantial clause or a new sentence; the verse teaches that learners should seek knowledge from the most expert and discerning teachers, even over long journeys.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p640#2/r3] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | What God taught means the knowledge of training, divinely inspired yet acquired through reason; alternatively it is what God showed people about sending, recalling, stopping, and retaining the catch for its owner.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p640#2/r4] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | reports | A variant reads mukallibīn with a lighter form; afʿala and faʿʿala often share a meaning.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p640#2/r5] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | In a sound report to ʿAdi ibn Hatim, the Prophet says not to eat the catch if the dog ate it, since it caught for itself.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p640#2/r6] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · علي | reports | Ali said not to eat the catch if a falcon ate from it.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p640#2/r7] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · العلماء | reports | Scholars differed: some require predatory beasts to refrain from eating because they can be trained by beating, but do not impose the condition on predatory birds.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p640#2/r8] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · بعض العلماء | reports | Some scholars do not treat eating as relevant and do not distinguish an animal holding all of the prey from holding only part.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p640#2/r9] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · سلمان وسعد بن أبي وقاص وأبو هريرة | reports | Salman, Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas, and Abu Hurayra allowed eating when a dog consumed two-thirds, left one-third, and God’s name had been invoked.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p640/r1] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | The indirect question means ‘they say to you, what has been made lawful for them’; the shift to third person follows the wording ‘they ask you,’ though first person would also be correct.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p640/r2] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | ‘What’ is the subject and ‘has been made lawful for them’ its predicate; the question concerns foods after prohibited foods were recited to them.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p640/r3] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | ‘Good things’ means what is not foul: anything not prohibited by scripture, the Sunna, or a jurist’s analogy.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p640/r4] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | The trained hunting animals may coordinate with ‘good things’ with an omitted word, meaning lawful food and game caught by your trained animals; alternatively, ‘what’ is conditional and ‘eat’ is its answer.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p640/r5] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | Jawāriḥ are hunting predators among beasts and birds, including dogs, leopards, tigers, eagles, falcons, and hawks.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p640/r6] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | Mukallib is the person who trains and disciplines hunting animals for their owner; the word derives from dogs because dogs are the most common, or because predators are called dogs.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p640/r7] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | The term can also derive from a predator being called a dog, or from keliba, ‘to be keenly attached’ to something.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p640/r8] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | To show that a predator is called a dog, the author cites a Prophetic supplication for God to set one of His dogs on a man; the animal was a lion.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p640/r9] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | The word can also mean keenly attached to something, as in describing someone as ‘a dog’ for it.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p641/r1] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | The pronoun in ‘mention God’s name over it’ can refer to the catch: invoke God when you find it alive and slaughter it.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p641/r2] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | Alternatively, the pronoun refers to the trained animal, so God’s name is invoked when it is sent out.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p156#2/r1] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · ابن عباس وأبو هريرة والشعبي وإبراهيم النخعي وسعيد بن جبير وعطاء بن أبي رباح وقتادة وعكرمة والشافعي وأحمد وإسحاق وأبو ثور والنعمان وأصحابه | reports | These authorities prohibit eating what remains when a dog eats the prey, because it held the prey for itself; they interpret “what they hold for you” as complete restraint and cite the Prophet's instruction to ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p156#2/r2] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · سعد بن أبي وقاص وعبد الله ابن عمر وأبو هريرة وسلمان الفارسي | reports | These authorities allow the remainder even if only a piece is left; Mālik and his followers read “what they hold for you” generally, so any amount of restraint suffices.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p156#2/r3] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · النخعي وأصحاب الرأي والثوري وحماد بن أبي سليمان | reports |

 They allow eating what a falcon has eaten from its catch, limiting this concession to falcons.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p156#2/r4] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | For a bird of prey, no more demanding training can be required than responding when called and going when sent.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p156#2/r5] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · جمهور الناس | reports | Most scholars allow the prey if the hunting animal drinks its blood; ʿAṭāʾ says drinking blood is not eating, while al-Shaʿbī and Sufyān al-Thawrī disapprove of that prey.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p156#2/r6] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Only a dog can be fully trained, and most animals eat their catch, so Mālik did not make abstaining from prey a condition of training.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p156#2/r7] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · ربيعة | reports | Rabīʿa says a bird is trained and predatory when it responds to being called.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p156/r1] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · أبو رافع | reports | The occasion was Gabriel's refusal to enter a house with a dog, the Prophet's order to kill dogs as far as al-ʿAwālī, and the three Companions' question about which dogs could be used; ʿIkrima and Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb also report it as a Companion-level account.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p156/r10] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · الحسن وقتادة وإبراهيم النخعي وأحمد بن حنبل وابن راهويه | reports | They disapprove of hunting with a solid-black dog; Aḥmad says he knows no one who permits it, while ordinary scholars in Medina and Kufa allow any trained dog.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p156/r2] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The apparent question concerns permitted foods, not keeping dogs; the answer may address more than asked, as the Prophet often expanded instruction while clarifying the law.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p156/r3] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | For Mālik and others, al-ṭayyibāt means lawful foods, whether or not they are pleasurable to eat.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p156/r4] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · الشافعي | reports | Al-Shāfiʿī takes al-ṭayyibāt to mean lawful and pleasurable foods, and treats repulsive animals such as geckos and beetles as forbidden filth.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p156/r5] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The highest training is for the dog to go when sent, return when called, stop after seizing prey when checked, and not eat the catch; a trained non-black dog used by a Muslim hunter and trained by a Muslim is agreed to be valid, while defects open disagreement.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p156/r6] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · جمهور الأمة | reports | The majority count any trained hunting animal, including a cheetah or a bird such as a falcon, as a jawāriḥ; Ibn ʿAṭiyya connects the term with earning or acquiring, as in 6:60. | mentions 6:60
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p156/r7] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · ابن عمر | reports | Ibn ʿUmar says hunting is only by dogs; a bird's catch is lawful only if its ritual slaughter is caught in time, a restriction also related from Abū Jaʿfar.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p156/r8] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · قوم | reports | Some permit falcons because of ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim's report that the Prophet said to eat what a falcon holds for the hunter.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p156/r9] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · الضحاك والسدي | reports | Al-Ḍaḥḥāk and al-Suddī restrict “jawāriḥ mukallibīn” to dogs.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p157#2/r1] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | rejects | Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the preceding explanation of mukallib is not precise.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p157#2/r10] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The general command to fear God points to all the commands contained in these verses.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p157#2/r11] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | God's reckoning is swift because He knows everything, needs no counting, and can reckon with all creatures at once.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p157#2/r12] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Alternatively, the verse warns that the Day of Judgment will arrive soon.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p157#2/r13] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Alternatively, swift reckoning means prompt retribution in this world if people fail to fear God.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p157#2/r2] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | “What you have taught” has an implied noun: the game or the keeping of the animals taught; their instruction includes hunting techniques and securing prey, and min can mean either a part or a point of origin.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p157#2/r3] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The feminine pronoun in “you teach them” follows the grammatical gender of jawāriḥ, the plural of jāriḥa.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p157#2/r4] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | “Eat what they hold for you” may mean prey from which they ate nothing, or any prey they held even if they ate some; this underlies the juristic disagreement.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p157#2/r5] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The command to name God applies when releasing the animal, under the same legal rules as naming God at slaughter.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p157#2/r6] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · الشعبي وابن سيرين ونافع وأبو ثور | reports | They dislike meat when God's name was omitted forgetfully, representing the strict view that omission prevents eating.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p157#2/r7] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · أشهب | reports | Ashhab treats naming as recommended: meat is forbidden if the omission shows contempt, but allowed when someone intentionally omitted it without knowing the rule and without neglecting the law.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p157#2/r8] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · مالك وجمهور أهل العلم | reports | They require naming when one remembers but excuse forgetfulness; deliberate omission invalidates prey or slaughter, while one who forgot names God at eating and the meat remains lawful.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p157#2/r9] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · أكثر أهل العلم | reports | Most scholars prefer that the formula name God alone and say “In God's name, God is greatest”; some permit adding a blessing on the Prophet.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p157/r1] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Ibn ʿAṭiyya explains Rabīʿa's criterion by noting that most animals naturally go when sent.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p157/r10] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · قوم | reports | Some derive jawāriḥ from an animal with a fang, claw, or talon that wounds its prey; Ibn ʿAṭiyya rejects this as weak and says the linguists disagree.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p157/r11] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · جمهور الناس | reports | The majority read mukallibīn with a doubled lām, meaning a trainer or instigator of dogs; the term can also describe someone training another animal by making it like a dog.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p157/r12] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · الحسن وأبو زيد | reports | They read with a still kāf and light lām, meaning owners of dogs, formed like a word for someone who has many of something.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p157/r13] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · بعض المفسرين | reports | Some commentators take the doubled-lām reading to mean a person who owns dogs.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p157/r2] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · أصحاب أبي حنيفة | reports | The Ḥanafī authorities count a dog as trained after it hunts and holds prey three times consecutively; al-Nuʿmān sets no number, while others require only one successful instance.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p157/r3] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · الحسن البصري | reports | Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī disapproves of hunting with a dog trained by a Jew or Christian.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p157/r4] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · جابر بن عبد الله والحسن وعطاء ومجاهد وإبراهيم النخعي والثوري وإسحاق بن راهويه | reports | They disapprove of hunting with a Zoroastrian's trained dog, falcon, or hawk.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p157/r5] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · مالك والشافعي وأبو حنيفة وأصحابهم | reports | They allow a Muslim to hunt with a Zoroastrian's trained animal, treating it like the hunter's knife.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p157/r6] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · جمهور الأمة | reports | Most authorities permit a People of the Book hunter, but Mālik forbids it, distinguishing hunting from slaughter and citing 5:94; Ibn Wahb and Ashhab allow it like their slaughter. | mentions 5:94
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p157/r7] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · محمد | reports | The Book of Muḥammad forbids the hunt and slaughter of Sabians, whom it describes as people between Jews and Christians with no religion.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p157/r8] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · مالك والشافعي وأبو حنيفة وأصحابهم وعطاء وابن جبير والنخعي والليث بن سعد وجمهور الناس | reports | They forbid eating a Zoroastrian's catch; Abū Thawr gives two positions, one agreeing and another treating Zoroastrians as People of the Book and permitting it.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p157/r9] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · ابن عباس ومحمد بن الحنفية | reports | They read “ʿallamtum” with ḍamma on the ʿayn and kasra on the lām, meaning the animals' hunting was taught or directed.

[TABRISI:5:4/r1] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The common reading is mukallibīn with a doubled lām; Ibn Masʿud and al-Hasan are reported to read it with a light lām.
[TABRISI:5:4/r10] TABRISI, d. 548 · أبو رافع | reports | When people asked what was lawful from the animals whose dogs they had been ordered to kill, the Prophet was silent and this verse was revealed; useful dogs were then permitted, while harmful or useless dogs were forbidden or killed.
[TABRISI:5:4/r11] TABRISI, d. 548 · أبو حمزة الثمالي، الحكم بن ظهيرة | reports | Abu Hamza al-Thumali and al-Hakam ibn Zahir report that Zayd al-Khayl and ʿAdi ibn Hatim asked about six dogs that caught wild cattle and gazelles, some alive and some dead; the verse allowed eating what they caught.
[TABRISI:5:4/r2] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Iklāb means inciting a dog to hunt and training it; mukallib can mean someone with many dogs or a dog hunter and trainer.

[TABRISI:5:4/r4] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | A line by al-Aʿshā uses jāriḥ for one who acquires; the poet’s line explains the word as earning.
[TABRISI:5:4/r5] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Mādhā aḥilla lahum has two parses: mā alone may be a noun with dhā as its predicate, or mādhā may be one subject with aḥilla as its predicate.

[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p417/r1] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · author | holds | Ṭayyibāt is plural of ṭayyib, opposite to foul; it describes what pleases the self, including food and scent, and figuratively what is lawful.

[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p290/r1] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | reports | One occasion report says the verse came after people asked what from the dogs they had been ordered to kill remained lawful; al-Hakim included it in his Sahih from Abu Rafiʿ, from the Prophet.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p290/r10] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · أبو سليمان الدمشقي | holds | Birds are trained differently from land predators: hunting birds are trained by eating, while dogs and cheetahs are trained by leaving the catch uneaten.

[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p290/r3] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · سعيد بن جبير | reports | A second occasion report says ʿAdi ibn Hatim and Zayd al-Khayl, whom the Prophet renamed Zayd al-Khayr, asked about their dog and falcon catches: some could be ritually slaughtered, others not, while carrion was forbidden.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p290/r4] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · الزجاج | holds | The question asks what is lawful; the answer supplies good things and the game caught by trained animals, with the latter phrase omitted because the context makes it clear.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p290/r5] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | reports | The two explanations of good things are permitted slaughtered animals, or what Arabs find good and palatable so long as it is not forbidden.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p290/r6] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | Jawarih are predatory land animals or birds used for hunting, such as dogs, cheetahs, falcons and hawks, that accept training; Ibn ʿAbbas says every hunting animal is a jarih.

[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p290/r8] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · الماوردي | reports | An alternative etymology calls them jawarih because they usually wound what they hunt.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p290/r9] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · أبو سليمان الدمشقي | reports | A trained beast answers when called, goes out when sent to hunt, and holds the catch for its owner rather than itself; not eating the catch is a sign of this.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p292/r1] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · أبو صالح، ابن عمر، سعيد بن جبير، عطاء، الضحاك، السدي، الفراء، الزجاج، ابن قتيبة | reports | Mukkalibin can mean owners of dogs; al-Zajjaj glosses mukallib or kilabi as a person who hunts with dogs.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p292/r10] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | On the preferred distinction, a dog or cheetah eating its catch makes it unlawful, while a falcon or hawk eating its catch remains lawful; Abu Hanifa and his school agree.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p292/r11] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · مالك | reports | Malik permits a catch eaten by a dog, cheetah or falcon, and permits a dog-killed catch if the dog did not eat it.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p292/r12] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · أبو حنيفة | reports | Abu Hanifa does not permit a dog-killed catch merely because the dog did not eat it; if live game dies before one can slaughter it, it is permitted, but if slaughter was possible it is not.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p292/r13] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · مالك، الشافعي، أبو حنيفة | reports | Malik and al-Shafiʿi permit game that dies after being caught alive when slaughter was not possible, but not when it was possible; Abu Hanifa permits neither case.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p292/r14] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · أحمد، الجمهور، الثوري | reports | Ahmad has one report that hunting with a Magian's dog is not disliked, as most authorities hold, and another report of dislike, as al-Thawri holds.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p292/r15] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · الثوري | reports | Al-Thawri objects to hunting with a Magian's dog because the address about trained game is directed to believers

[RAZI-FULL:v11p112/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Pre-Islamic Arabs forbade some wholesome foods such as baḥīra, sāʾiba, waṣīla, and ḥām on weak grounds; the verse declares wholesome things lawful. | mentions 7:32, 7:157

[RAZI-FULL:v11p113#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The verse requires hunting animals to be trained; the Prophet told ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim to eat from prey caught by a trained dog after pronouncing God's name.

[RAZI-FULL:v11p113#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · أبو حنيفة | reports | In another report from Abū Ḥanīfa, an animal is trained after two repetitions; Aḥmad also holds this view.
[RAZI-FULL:v11p113#2/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · أبو يوسف ومحمد | reports | Abū Yūsuf and Muḥammad require three repetitions for training.
[RAZI-FULL:v11p113#2/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · صاحب الكشاف | reports | Al-Zamakhsharī reports a lightened reading of mukallibīn and notes that the forms afʿala and faʿʿala often share a meaning.

[RAZI-FULL:v11p113/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | An alternative analysis takes the hunting-animal clause as a new sentence whose predicate is the command to eat what the animals catch, requiring no ellipsis.
[RAZI-FULL:v11p113/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | Jawāriḥ may mean animals that acquire prey, from the verb for earning or acquiring, as in the cited Qur'anic usages. | mentions 45:21, 6:60
[RAZI-FULL:v11p113/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | Another lexical view derives jawāriḥ from wounding; on that view, prey taken without drawing blood is not lawful.
[RAZI-FULL:v11p113/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · ابن عمر | reports | Ibn ʿUmar, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, and al-Suddī are reported to disallow prey caught by a non-dog predator if the hunter does not reach it in time to slaughter it.
[RAZI-FULL:v11p113/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الليث | reports | Al-Layth reports Mujāhid's view that falcons, hawks, eagles, leopards, and other hunting predators all count as jawāriḥ.
[RAZI-FULL:v11p113/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | Defenders of non-dog hunting answer that mukallibīn can mean training all hunting animals, a term derived from dogs because dogs are commonly trained.
[RAZI-FULL:v11p113/r8] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | They also argue that every predatory animal may be called a dog, citing the Prophet's prayer that a dog among God's dogs be sent against a man, whom a lion then killed.
[RAZI-FULL:v11p113/r9] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | A third answer derives kalb from the sense of eagerness: someone intensely desirous of something is described as kalib for it.
[RAZI-FULL:v11p114/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | If a trained dog wounds and kills prey found dead by the hunter, it is lawful; the animal's wound counts as slaughter, as with other trained predators, arrows, and spears.
[RAZI-FULL:v11p114/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | If a dog kills by crushing without wounding, some call the prey carrion, while others permit it under the rule allowing what hunting animals catch for their owner.
[RAZI-FULL:v11p114/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās, Ṭāwūs, al-Shaʿbī, ʿAṭāʾ, al-Suddī, and the predominant Shāfiʿī view forbid prey partly eaten by the hunting animal because it caught the prey for itself, not its owner.
[RAZI-FULL:v11p114/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet told ʿAdī: if prey is found dead and uneaten, eat it because the dog held it for you; if the dog ate from it, do not eat because it held it for itself.
[RAZI-FULL:v11p114/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · سلمان الفارسي | reports | Salman, Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ, Ibn ʿUmar, and Abū Hurayra permit the prey even if the animal ate; this is al-Shāfiʿī's second view.

[QURTUBI-FULL:5:4#3/r12] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Jawāriḥ means earners; the view that it means animals that wound and bleed is weak and contrary to the linguists, though Ibn al-Mundhir attributes it to some.

[QURTUBI-FULL:5:4#3/r15] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The verb aklaba means a persons dogs multiplied, illustrating the reading as dog owners.

[QURTUBI-FULL:5:4#3/r6] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · جماعة من أصحابنا | reports | Other scholars in the Maliki school and elsewhere allow eating the Muslim’s hunted or slaughtered animal even if the basmala was deliberately omitted, treating the command as recommendation.

[QURTUBI-FULL:5:4#4/r11] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · مالك | reports | Malik and his school, along with one Shafii opinion, accept the second view; al-Qurtubi calls it analogical.

[QURTUBI-FULL:5:4#6/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Do not eat prey mixed with dogs other than the one named over, because the hunter named only his own dog.

[QURTUBI-FULL:5:4/r10] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The root “jaraḥa” means to acquire, as in the verse about what people earn by day and the verse about those who have earned sins. | mentions 6:60, 45:21
[QURTUBI-FULL:5:4/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | In “what has been made lawful to them,” “ma” may be the subject with “has been made lawful to them” as predicate, and “dha” is extra; alternatively “ma-dha” is a relative pronoun with the answer as predicate.

[QURTUBI-FULL:5:4/r7] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The community agrees on the conditions for a trained nonblack dog: it responds to release and call, stops when rebuked after catching prey, does not eat the prey, wounds it, and is released by a Muslim invoking God’s name.

[BAYDAWI-FULL:5:3-5/r18] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | God-consciousness here means observing God's prohibitions; He quickly reckons and holds people to account for both major and minor matters.

[BURSEVI:v2p275/r5] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | الجوارح is a circumstantial phrase and plural of جارحة, meaning an acquiring animal; it may also derive from wounding, since hunting animals often tear prey. | mentions 6:60
[BURSEVI:v2p275/r6] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The term covers any trainable animal that catches game for its owner, including hunting mammals such as cheetahs, leopards, and dogs, and birds such as falcons and eagles; their catches are lawful.

[BURSEVI:v2p275/r8] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Calling the trainers مكلبين stresses their expertise: the title applies only to a highly skilled trainer, so the phrase means they are adept and renowned in training.
[BURSEVI:v2p275/r9] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | تعلمونهن is a second circumstantial phrase; God taught people the techniques of training, whether by inspiration, reason as a divine gift, or learned methods such as sending, calling back, stopping, and having the animal hold prey without eating it.
[BURSEVI:v2p276/r1] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · صاحب الكشاف | reports | Al-Kashshaf says the verse teaches that students should learn from a deeply expert master who knows a field's subtleties, even if reaching that teacher requires a long journey.
[BURSEVI:v2p276/r10] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · أنس رضي الله عنه | reports | Anas reports that the Prophet sacrificed two white, horned rams by his own hand, saying God's name and magnifying Him.
[BURSEVI:v2p276/r11] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The recommended formula is بسم الله الله أكبر without و because the conjunction would cut off the light of the basmala, according to Sharh Mukhtasar al-Wiqaya.
[BURSEVI:v2p276/r12] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Leaving the qibla orientation is disliked, while the sacrifice remains valid, as stated in al-Dhakhira.
[BURSEVI:v2p276/r13] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Deliberately omitting God's name makes the animal carrion and forbidden, while forgetting to invoke it leaves the meat lawful.
[BURSEVI:v2p276/r14] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Taqwa here means observing God's prohibitions; سريع الحساب means either that reckoning arrives soon or that it is completed quickly once begun, so God accounts for every small and great matter swiftly.

[BURSEVI:v2p276/r3] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Learning from someone unqualified wastes one's days and leaves one regretting it when meeting the true experts.
[BURSEVI:v2p276/r4] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The partitive من means eat some of what the animal held, omitting inedible hides, bones, and feathers; the relative pronoun has an omitted antecedent, and على marks what was held for the hunter.
[BURSEVI:v2p276/r5] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Eat only the prey the trained animal has not eaten; if it ate from the prey, it held it for itself, as the Prophet told ʿAdi ibn Hatim, and most jurists agree.

[BURSEVI:v2p276/r7] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · بعضهم ومنهم أبو حنيفة | reports | Some jurists, including Abu Hanifa, allow the remainder of prey caught by a trained bird but not by a dog, since a dog can be trained not to eat by beating whereas a hawk cannot.
[BURSEVI:v2p276/r8] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The pronoun in واذكروا اسم الله عليه may refer to what was trained, requiring invocation when releasing it, or to the prey held, requiring invocation when slaughtering it.
[BURSEVI:v2p276/r9] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | In Abu Thaʿlaba's report, the Prophet says to avoid the People of the Book's utensils if alternatives exist, or wash them if not; eat game taken with a bow or trained dog when God's name was invoked, and eat an untrained dog's catch only if it is found alive and slaughtered.
[BURSEVI:v2p277#2/r1] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The good things are those that sound, cultivated natures do not find repugnant.
[BURSEVI:v2p277#2/r2] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Alternatively, good things are those no revealed text or juristic analogy establishes as forbidden.

[ALUSI-FULL:v1p10/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Kalam can mean the act of speaking or the utterance produced by it; linguistically the word primarily names the product, whether much or little and literal or figurative, though al-Raḍī notes its use for the act.
[ALUSI-FULL:v1p10/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Each sense has a verbal and a mental form: verbal speech is the act of the tongue or the quality of audible sound; mental speech is the mind’s unexpressed act or its imagined, internally ordered words.
[ALUSI-FULL:v1p10/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · أم سلمة | reports | Al-Ṭabarānī reports from Umm Salama that a man asked the Prophet about an inward thought he feared would ruin his reward; the Prophet called it speech and said only a believer receives it.
[ALUSI-FULL:v1p10/r6] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | A sacred hadith saying God remembers the servant who remembers Him inwardly supports mental speech in both its act and content senses, for servant and Lord, while their realities remain incomparable.
[ALUSI-FULL:v1p10/r7] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | God’s mental speech in its first sense is an eternal attribute opposed to an inner defect like muteness, not made of letters or words, and one in essence despite varied objects of relation.
[ALUSI-FULL:v1p10/r8] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The relation of divine speech to a newly occurring object does not make the attribute itself temporal; the author accepts renewal only in the relation’s occurrence.

[ALUSI-FULL:v6p62#2/r10] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · قائلون | reports | Another definition is anything for which no text or analogy establishes a prohibition; consensus also falls within this view because it must rest on textual evidence.
[ALUSI-FULL:v6p62#2/r11] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | On the latter two definitions “wholesome” means lawful, while on the first it means pleasant; Arabic usage supports both senses.
[ALUSI-FULL:v6p62#2/r12] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | One grammatical analysis coordinates “what you train” with wholesome things as a relative clause, supplying an omitted “catch”; another treats it as the source of catching, a specific case under the general permission.
[ALUSI-FULL:v6p62#2/r13] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | prefers | Al-Ālūsī says the apparent reading needs no implied “catch,” because permissibility and prohibition attach to actions.
[ALUSI-FULL:v6p62#2/r14] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | Alternatively, “what” is conditional and the following command is its response, coordinated with the sentence “the wholesome things are made lawful for you.”
[ALUSI-FULL:v6p62#2/r15] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhsharī allows an implied noun even with conditional “what,” since a noun annexed to a conditional expression has the same grammatical status as the expression itself.
[ALUSI-FULL:v6p62#2/r16] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The implied-noun analysis is challenged because the predicate would then need an understood referent, unless “what they caught” is made to stand in place of “what you trained.”
[ALUSI-FULL:v6p62#2/r17] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | A further, less apparent analysis treats “what” as a relative pronoun and “eat” as its predicate, with the prefixed faʾ inserted by analogy to a conditional clause.
[ALUSI-FULL:v6p62#2/r18] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · أبو البقاء | reports | Abū al-Baqāʾ takes the hāʾ in “jawāriḥ” as an intensive feminine ending; the word is commonly used without an expressed noun.
[ALUSI-FULL:v6p62#2/r19] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | “Jawāriḥ” means acquisitive beasts of prey and birds, either because they earn for their owners or because they commonly wound prey.
[ALUSI-FULL:v6p62#2/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · أبو رافع | reports | Abū Rāfiʿ reports that Gabriel delayed entering because a house contained an image or dog; after a puppy was found, the Prophet ordered dogs killed in Medina, and people’s question about what remained lawful occasioned the verse.
[ALUSI-FULL:v6p62#2/r20] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · ابن عمر، السدي، الضحاك، أئمة أهل البيت | reports | Ibn ʿUmar, al-Suddī, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, and a report ascribed to the Imams of the Prophet’s family restrict “jawāriḥ” to dogs.
[ALUSI-FULL:v6p62#2/r21] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | “Mukallibīn” means training the hunting animals; the term derives from the dog because it is commonly trained, or because every beast of prey may be called a dog.
[ALUSI-FULL:v6p62#2/r22] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · أبو نوفل | reports | Abū Nawfal reports that a lion killed Lahab ibn Abī Lahab after the Prophet prayed for a “dog” to be set upon him; al-Ḥākim graded the report sound in chain, though al-Ālūsī says it does not show birds are included.
[ALUSI-FULL:v6p62#2/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · عكرمة | reports | ʿIkrima identifies the questioners as ʿĀṣim ibn ʿAdī, Saʿd ibn Khaythama, and ʿUwaym ibn Sāʿida.
[ALUSI-FULL:v6p62#2/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · ابن جبير | reports | Ibn Jubayr instead names ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim and Zayd ibn al-Muhalhil al-Ṭāʾī as the questioners.
[ALUSI-FULL:v6p62#2/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The question embeds the meaning of a statement, so its answer is quoted as a clause; the verb governs the clause because asking causes and leads to knowledge, contrary to Abū Ḥayyān.
[ALUSI-FULL:v6p62#2/r6] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · أبو حيان | reports | Abū Ḥayyān disagrees that the question verb can govern the clause; some grammarians posit an omitted noun, “the answer to what was made lawful.”
[ALUSI-FULL:v6p62#2/r7] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | The prior context suggests they ask which foods and meals are permitted; another view takes the question to concern game and slaughter.
[ALUSI-FULL:v6p62#2/r8] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · البلخي | reports | Al-Balkhī defines wholesome things as those that sound human dispositions do not find disgusting or recoil from.
[ALUSI-FULL:v6p62#2/r9] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · أبو علي الجبائي، أبو مسلم | reports | Abū ʿAlī al-Jubbāʾī and Abū Muslim define wholesome things as foods, sacrifices, and game God has authorized people to eat.
[ALUSI-FULL:v6p63#2/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | In “from what God taught you,” the preposition may indicate cause or mean “some of what God taught you.”
[ALUSI-FULL:v6p63#2/r10] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · إمام الحرمين | reports | Imām al-Ḥaramayn, a Shāfiʿī, follows the distinction that tolerates a hunting bird’s eating its prey.
[ALUSI-FULL:v6p63#2/r11] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · مالك، الليث | reports | Mālik and al-Layth permit eating the catch even when the dog has eaten from it.
[ALUSI-FULL:v6p63#2/r12] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · سلمان، سعد بن أبي وقاص، أبو هريرة | reports | Salman, Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ, and Abū Hurayra are reported to permit the catch if the dog ate two-thirds, a third remains, and God’s name was invoked.
[ALUSI-FULL:v6p63#2/r13] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · ابن عباس، الحسن، السدي | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, and al-Suddī take “invoke God’s name over it” to mean saying the name when releasing the trained animal.
[ALUSI-FULL:v6p63#2/r14] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | Others refer the pronoun to the caught animal and say the name if it is found alive and slaughtered; a further, less likely view refers it to the act of eating, as Abū Ḥayyān prefers.
[ALUSI-FULL:v6p63#2/r15] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · أبو حنيفة، الشافعي | reports | Abū Ḥanīfa regards invoking God’s name as obligatory, while al-Shāfiʿī regards it as recommended; on the eating-time interpretation, it is recommended by agreement.

[ALUSI-FULL:v6p63/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | Another etymology derives “mukallibīn” from kalb meaning avidity: someone may be called avid for something, and the participle describes the trainer.

[IBNASHUR-FULL:v6p111/r8] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · محمد الكاكي | reports | In the Hanafi Sharḥ al-Hidāya, Muḥammad al-Kākī reports the rule that what Arabs find pleasant is lawful and what they find repugnant is forbidden. | mentions 7:157
